conservationStatus.scope: The 2025 regional Red List for South Africa, Eswatini and Lesotho (NT C2a(ii)). The IUCN global assessment lists the species as Least Concern.

sources.title: Spotted Hyaena
sources.note: Regional status Near Threatened C2a(ii); regional trend stable.

size.note: Shoulder height of 70–91.5 cm and body length of 95–165.8 cm follow the Wikipedia dimensions section (bounds rounded to the nearest centimetre). Animal Diversity Web gives a narrower shoulder height of about 75–85 cm and a shorter body length of about 95–150 cm; the Wikipedia ranges are entered and the disagreement is noted. Tail length of 30–36 cm is from Animal Diversity Web only; Wikipedia did not publish a tail range. Sexed mass follows the Wikipedia Serengeti ranges: males 40.5–55.0 kg and females 44.5–63.9 kg (rounded to 40–55 and 44–64 kg). Animal Diversity Web gives males of about 45–60 kg and females of 55 to over 70 kg. Wikipedia also gives heavier Zambia averages of 67.6 kg (males) and 69.2 kg (females), which are averages and are not entered as ranges; southern animals may therefore be heavier than the Serengeti ranges. No Kruger-specific mass was found. Females are larger than males.

summary: Kruger's most often seen large scavenger-hunter: a powerfully built, spotted hyaena with a sloping back, rounded ears and a large head. It lives in matriarchal clans, hunts as well as scavenges, and is famous for its whoops and laugh-like giggles.
description: The largest living hyaena. The coat is a pale greyish-brown or yellowish-grey, marked with an irregular pattern of roundish reddish, brown or almost black spots on the back and hindquarters; the spots are less distinct on the legs and belly, and are absent from the throat and chest. The fur is shorter than in the brown hyaena, and there is only a modest crest on the neck rather than a long shaggy mane. The ears are rounded, the muzzle is blackish, and there is a pale band above the eyes. The front legs are longer than the hind legs, so the back slopes down to a short tail with a bushy black tip. Females are larger than males. Unusually among mammals, the female has a pseudo-penis and gives birth through it. Cubs are born with a soft, dark brown coat, and the spots develop as they grow.
habits: Highly social, living in matriarchal clans that may number from a few animals to several dozen. Females are dominant over males, and rank is inherited. Clans hunt cooperatively as well as scavenge, and they defend a territory. They are active by day and night, but are often seen at dawn, dusk and at kills or waterholes. A clan's social life is noisy and competitive, especially at a carcass.

diet.summary: The most carnivorous of the hyaenas, and primarily a hunter, though it also scavenges and can digest skin and bone. In Kruger its most important prey are blue wildebeest, buffalo, Burchell's zebra, kudu and impala; giraffe are also taken in the adjoining Timbavati area. Unlike some other large carnivores, it does not specialise on one prey species.

young: Gestation averages about 110 days (about four months). The average litter is two cubs, with three reported occasionally; Animal Diversity Web also gives a range of one to four, usually twins. Cubs are born with their eyes open and with a soft, dark brown coat, and they may attack one another shortly after birth. Females give birth through a narrow clitoris (the pseudo-penis), which ruptures during birth and may take weeks to heal. Males take no part in raising the young. Cubs are weaned at about 14–18 months. Mating is described as aseasonal. In the subregion young are born throughout the year with a peak in late summer, and in Kruger the average gap between litters was found to be about 16–19 months (Skinner and Chimimba 2005, pp. 376–377). A Kruger-specific birth-month range was not found.
habitat: Open and mixed savanna, woodland and grassland, including areas near waterholes, kills and rest camps. It is widespread in Kruger and is one of the large carnivores most often seen from a vehicle.

similar.note: The brown hyaena has a long, shaggy dark-brown coat, a pale neck ruff, pointed ears and striped legs, not a short spotted coat and rounded ears.
The aardwolf is much smaller and slimmer, with a yellowish, vertically striped coat, a long erectile mane and a slender muzzle, not a spotted coat or a massive bone-crushing head.

population.notes: Some sources claim a 2015 Kruger call-up survey estimated 7,339 spotted hyaenas (6,998–7,680) (S. Ferreira unpublished data, cited on the EWT 2025 assessment). The same page also states a 55% mature subset of 3,849–4,224, in one place labelled as adults and subadults; the detailed text treats 7,339 (6,998–7,680) as the 2015 estimate of individuals. Call-up counts are underestimates. The increase from 2005 to 2015 is described as genuine, using the same method and matching a rise in prey biomass. There has been no later park-wide figure in the sources consulted. The official aerial census sheet covers large herbivores, not this survey. The EWT 2025 assessment lists the regional trend as stable and says the Kruger subpopulation does not appear to be threatened, though disease or climate change could yet reduce it.

head.face: crown and upper face brownish, with a pale band above the eyes; the muzzle, lips and back of the chin blackish

mane.shape: a modest forward-facing crest on the neck, much shorter than the mane of a brown hyaena or an aardwolf

upperparts.pattern: irregular roundish reddish, brown or almost black spots on the back and hindquarters; five faint pale bands on the neck

underparts.pattern: spots less distinct on the belly; throat and chest unspotted

legs.colour: spotted; front legs longer than the hind legs, so the back slopes down

upperparts.pattern: spots absent or only beginning to appear as the cub grows

viewNotes.note: A large head, rounded ears, a pale band above the eyes and a blackish muzzle.
A sloping back, a spotted coat, a short black-tipped tail and a modest neck crest.
A dark brown, almost unspotted coat distinguishes a young cub from the spotted adult.

calls.description: An extensive range of sounds, including whoops, fast whoops, grunts, groans, lows, giggles, yells, growls, grunt-laughs, whines and soft squeals. The loud who-oop and the laugh-like giggle are the most widely recognised. High-pitched calls tend to signal fear or submission, and louder, lower calls aggression. The pitch of the laugh can indicate age, and the pattern of notes can indicate social rank. Whoops also carry signatures that can identify individuals. The Kruger recordings below do not name the call type.
